title: The Appearance of Light - Encouragement for the New Year
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach's main teaching is about cultivating a calm and accepting mind by embracing all experiences in the present moment, without resistance or struggle. This allows us to find our authentic self and function in harmony with the world around us, leading to a sense of peace and connection that dissolves distinctions between ourselves and others. By letting go of control and judgment, we can tap into a deeper sense of understanding and kindness towards others, and receive new experiences that bring us closer to our true nature.

sentences.text: **Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Good evening.
This feels really good.
Somehow this feels really appropriate for the talk at the end of the year, doesn't it?
I feel like we're in our little winter cave or ego somewhere, cozied up.
The title of this talk is something like "The Appearance of Light, Encouragement for the New Year."
Solstice just passed, and I think we celebrate solstice because it's the longest night of the year, which means it's soon going to start to get a little bit lighter.
That feels really good.
And it's no wonder at Christmas time that there are all of these colored lights that we put on our Christmas trees.
No matter what your faith, it's a marker of this time of year that we're surrounded by light.

I don't know about your experience growing up, but I know my experience was that at Christmas time there were all kinds of lights on the tree, and it was a time of gathering together, much as we are here, in a kind of quietude and warmth and friendliness.
It was a time of relative peace and harmony.
It's like everyone felt it around us, on the streets, in the stores, in our homes.
My grandmother baked.
Christmas was really simple and warm-hearted.
That kind of feeling is so encouraging.
I was thinking about what it was like for Siddhartha when he sat under the rose apple tree as a little boy.
And I bet it was that very simple, similar kind of peacefulness, like everything is just right and in its place, with no worries in the world.
Where I live right now, I look out on one end of Lake Whatcom.
During this time of year, across the lake, which isn't so far away, everyone has their lights on.
The lights shine on the lake and form a multitude of small points as the waves go very slowly.
My neighbors have their bright Christmas lights on, and they too reflect in my windows, and they reflect off the lake.
It's so peaceful, and it's so encouraging, and it's so beautiful.
I think that's what we hope for when we come to sit here, isn't it?
To find that kind of peace and calm and ease.
The way the light shines in here, it's just this soft warmth.
We'd like to have a calm mind entering into the new year and facing the challenges that are before us.
You ask yourself, what really is a calm mind?
We think we know what it is when we sit.
We think it's quiet.
There's no activity.
There's nothing that really bothers us inside that calm mind.
But actually, there's nothing that comes from the outside that isn't already in our mind.
It doesn't arrive with the Christmas lights or the quiet of the lake.
Sometimes, especially in our first years of sitting, we try to push away those thoughts that we don't particularly like.
They're upsetting.
They're dissonant.
If we can just quiet them down, we'll find that peaceful place.
And if we try to do that, it actually creates more waves in our mind.
You ever notice that?
It's like the ripples on the lake.
If we put a barrier out there to try and stop the ripples, it actually creates bigger waves.
So we're actually rocking the waves of aversion: "Go away."
It creates more waves.
What would happen if we actually accepted that which we don't want?
What if we actually accepted the pain that comes up in our knee, the circling thoughts, anxieties, stories, difficulties?
What if we actually let that all in, allowed all of it to be just part of one big piece of our lives?
Because that's what that really is.
That's actually what our zazen is, isn't it?
When you sit quietly and you really settle, everything that emerges in your life is part of that one piece of zazen.
It arises and manifests itself and reveals itself and it changes.
When we sit in our posture with the Buddha Mudra, our hands together, resting lightly, thumbs lightly touching, the Buddha Mudra is actually manifesting Buddha, is being Buddha as we sit just now.
That light arises accepting everything.
We receive the pain in the knees, the drone of repetitive thoughts, the storylines, accept the anger, the hopelessness, the anxiety, and allow it to become just it.
Without struggling, it stops.
It finds its own proper place.
It finds its own proper level.
It's rather like being in the breath, coming back to the breath, as natural as waves on the shore.
The shore of the ocean does not resist the return of the waves, and the waves don't need to resist returning back to the sea.
The sea receives them.

That's how it is in our mind with our thoughts, with the sensations when we sit zazen, and the breath becomes a reliable presence, just like the waves on Lake Whatcom, just like the waves on the ocean.
The world is no longer split.
It's no longer split into that which we like or don't like, that which we're striving for, that which we're trying to leave.
It's no longer split between the small mind, which is our usual way of being and thinking about things and creating ourselves, that which has an inside and an outside.

It becomes part of one big piece, a big mind, which contains everything, and it takes its natural place in the world, an intimate part of the workings of things as it is, to use the words of Suzuki Roshi.
This is the very foundation of this school, of the Soto Zen school.
There's an image, I think it's in the Platform Sutra, where Hui Nang is talking about Bodhidharma rising to the platform to give his seat and turning into the sun.
He turns into this big pulsating light, and in my early years sitting I thought, wow, how'd he do that?
What kind of altered mind state is that?
He was transmitting light.
He was being light sitting in zazen.

Hongshu and his teachings on silent illumination, an objectless meditation that you all studied during Rohatsu, that is the essence of this stillness, allowing all things to manifest in this moment and verify themselves.

He was the foundational teacher for Dogen's teacher, and Dogen's great jewel that he took from China and whisked off to Japan, that was our zazen, our shikantaza, that which we sit and illuminate light, the light like the full moon swallowing up the whole of Lake Whatcom, just like that.
Dogen describes this so well in one of the first pieces he wrote when he returned from China, in Bendoa.
Bendoan is a love song to shikantaza, to this kind of silent illumination, total light.
He talks about the upright posture and simple sitting that is the practice of every Soto Zen temple.
He describes it as Jijyusamai.
Jijyusamai means self-fulfilling and receiving samadhi.
It's just exactly what we've been talking about, that sitting still and allowing yourself to receive everything, verifying your place in the world, verifying your very existence.
Dogen says:
*When one displays the Buddha Mudra with one's whole body and mind sitting upright in the samadhi, even for a short time, everything in the entire world becomes the Buddha Mudra.
Everything illuminates light and all space in the universe completely becomes enlightenment.*

Because of this mutual resonance, Dogen is saying that not only teachers help the practitioner, but there's an imperceptible guidance and assistance between space, between everything itself and the person sitting.
Zazen influences not only the person around the practitioner, but also grass, trees, fences, walls, and pebbles.
Everything becomes light.
We sitting verify everything and everything verifies us.
Uchiyama Roshi says that sitting zazen, this Jijyusamai, is actually the self becoming, making the self into the self.
The self making the self into the self.
So really recognizing sitting zazen, recognizing becoming your authentic manifestation in that moment.
Your authentic full manifestation in that self, so that the self is functioning.
This person, this reality sitting before you, each reality here is functioning in its proper role in this moment.
Isn't that reassuring?
Isn't that reassuring, if you show up and receive everything that you've been given?
Everything, the troubles in your minds, the mind weeds, the delusions, everything, receiving it.
That's your total functioning in that moment.
When we take our place or our function in this point in time, in this place, it's like being plugged into the energy source.
Like the glow of Christmas, like the return of light.
This is our task, to take our place, which is not a place that can be sought in the usual ways.
But we know it when we sit zazen.
I'd say we know it when we feel it.
Sometimes I look out at the lights on Lake Whatcom and the wind is blowing, because it blows kind of hard out at that end of the lake sometimes.
The lights are all dispersed and the waters all churned up.
At first that seems like it spoils it.
It spoils those beautiful dots of light.
It mixes up all the colors.
But how I see them and how I respond to them is the working of just my ideas.
Just my ideas about what I like and what I don't like.
It's just my conditioned ideas and experience.
Seen for what they are, as reflections on the moving water, they're not disturbances, but just part of the fabric of the moment.
I think we know this acceptance.
Siddhartha felt it under the rose apple tree.
Maybe you did the first time you really sat meditation, or when you go out and walk in the mountains after it snowed.
Suzuki Roshi called it a religious feeling.
I think it's a truing of ourselves with life.
Truing, meaning being totally in sync, totally rolling along just perfectly without any wobble.
Nothing's out of place.
Nothing to disturb.
This is what we call big mind.
We recognize intuitively that big and small mind are one, and in fact because we are no longer blocking the waves, instead of being disturbed, our mind is amplified by the waves.
It's expanded by the waves.
There's Jijuyu Samae, and then there's Taju Yu Samae.
There's self-fulfilling and receiving samadhi, and there's other fulfilling and receiving samadhi.
The other is the affirmation of everything coming forward in the same moment.
All the different lights dancing on the water, all coming together in that moment, creating it.
Affirming this life by affirming everything together.
Because we are no longer blocking out the waves, instead of being disturbed, our mind is amplified.
It includes everything, and it flows freely.
It's more aligned.
At the very last talk he gave to a group of his intimate students he had practiced with for twenty or thirty years, Kobun Chino was asked, "Why do we sit zazen?"
It's a question apparently that he was asked many times over the years, and he had tried to answer, and his students asked him again this time.
They didn't know it would be his last talk.
He died suddenly and tragically not long thereafter.
In that talk he said that we sit zazen to be a candle in the dark, to manifest this light in the midst of the dark, in the midst of the confusion, in the midst of the not knowing.

This time of year, the new year, before the light returns, we often take the time to think about what that light is in our own life, what we aspire to, what we hope for the year, for our families, for our community, for our nation, for ourselves, and what our part in it is.
What's the light of our candle in this time?
For myself, it's interesting.

Many times later this year people have come and they will confide, sometimes at the end of a visit, that they just don't know what to do in these times, that they feel the burden of the difficulty that people feel, the vulnerability, the impossibility of it all.
My teacher said recently, when you face a question that you don't know how to answer, what do you say to someone who's facing it like us every day?
What do I do in this difficult time?
He said, "Dig deeper."
Dig deeper.
It means to find that place in your hara, the place that you touch in zazen where the breath arises like the waves on the shore meeting and returning.
Dig deeper to that place that you don't really know but you experience, and connect from there.
What seems to me the answer now is to be kind, to be very, very kind.

Not the kind of kindness of being nice, not the kind of kindness of being helpful or charitable, but the kindness that understands how impossible it is, the kindness that understands what human misery is about, the kindness that sees the pictures of the Syrian refugees on the shore and wants to understand that people experience those things.
To be very, very kind.
Not long ago, I think this last week, I was thinking, but that's not enough, actually.
Or there's another dimension there, not that it's not enough, and I think it comes from understanding that things end, this life ends.
When I was at Berkeley recently, I was sitting in the zendo, a small group of people.
A third of the people were seventy or older, a third were between sixty and seventy, a small percentage were younger than that, and the teacher almost ninety.

We've been sitting together forever, and I sure remember people when they were a whole lot younger, including me, and I remember the people who aren't there anymore, whether they've died or they've come and gone.

All of time passed, kind of like when Buddha sat under the Bodhi tree and the night that he awakened, all his past lifetimes appeared, and you recognize, oh, all of this changes, all of this ends, all of this moves on.
Oh, what's left?
Fearlessness.
Fearlessness is what's left.
It's not the kind of fearlessness where you're not afraid, it's the kind of fearlessness that says, this is it.
What's here in front of me now?
This is it.
Okay.
There's nothing to lose.
It all changes.
It all ends.
What's the answer right now?
That's my candle in the dark.

And I wonder about you, if you take a few moments right now and you think about what that is, how that feels, what manifests for you when you sit in your body, in your aura, in your experience of zazen.
What does it mean to you to be a candle in the dark?
We're not quite out of time, so maybe I'll ask you to say something.
Maybe each of you will have a word or a sentence or two that you want to share.
You don't have to.
You can pass.
But don't try too hard.
Just say something.
**Participant:** Yeah, I would say to try to bring some calm along with whatever my action might be in a situation. [unclear: "A good action is a mistake."] To still have some calmness.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** I think it's not just what we do, right, but how we do it.
It's the mind, the heart, and the presence with which we do something that matters so much more than actually what the thing is that we do.
**Participant:** You just said what I have thought, and that is being present, showing up.
I find myself interacting with people, whether it's at the grocery store or the checkout counter, to kind of look them straight in the eye and thank them for their service and thank them for helping.
They say, "How are you doing?"
I say, "How are you doing?"

I try to engage people on a one-to-one basis with kindness, because the larger picture is so difficult to even figure out where to put a hook into it that I'm kind of working on the one-to-one moment-by-moment relationship.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Thank you.

**Participant:** What Bob was talking about, and when I'm in a real good place and can think about doing it, when I interact with anyone, maybe the person on the checkout counter or just anybody, concentrate on just looking them in the eye and talking to them, because I don't do that very much and I have to make an effort to do that.
But when I do, there's a connection and I feel much better and more peace, and I think probably they do too, and I kind of wonder why I can't do that more, but I'll keep working at it.
**Participant:** Just to add to the presence of myself, to slow down and be present.
Presence is what is needed in our speeded-up world.
It feels so speedy and so full, to truly be able to sink and be present with all that seems to be moving increasingly in a speedy way.
I want to speed up too, and sometimes the speeding up is not because I get into that slipstream but because I want to just get through it and get past it.
So to just slow down and be present is a candle that I'd like to practice bringing.
**Participant:** I'm pretty disturbed by what's going on in this country.

It infiltrates almost every day of mine, like a lot of us I think, and I have really been aware of how much these people that I tend to blame are really suffering so much, and you can really see how that's true.
So I bring that out and it really softens things for me and it softens my relationship to that.
So let's spend practice in that.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** I think that's what Sojun meant when he said dig deeper.
Find the human connection.
Find the ground that you both stand on and respond from that place.
It's personal.
It looks people in the eye.
It's curious.
It's warm-hearted.
It's slowed down to make that connection, to be willing to drop enough of our ideas or judgments to say, what is that for you?
**Participant:** It's trusting.
I think a lot about trust.
Practice especially this next year, trusting the situation, trusting myself, trusting the person.
Setting down some of that kind of agitated energy of trying to sort of control, which is sort of a non-trust.
Make space.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** That's really beautiful and I think it's really to the heart of the teaching of Tadayusamai.
Trust is, I'm not, you know, this isn't something I'm doing.
I'm not creating this.
This is happening here all together now, and I trust that.
I trust the natural harmony of things coming together.

I don't know if you've been aware of having these experiences, but when you get out of the way, you get your ideas out of the way of a situation, you're really willing to receive everything that's there.
Amazing things happen that you had no idea about in your limited view.
**Participant:** That's what I was thinking about, the candle in the dark.
That could be kind of scary.
I think that's hard and lonely, but it works better if I just allow the expression of something bigger than me to be just coming through this perspective.
To answer you personally on that question for that statement.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Yes, and our function.
Each of us has our function as the candle.
That's true, and each of us has our function as the candle to manifest.
Is there anyone who hasn't spoken who wants to say something?
All of you.
And any other words anyone wants to add?
**Participant:** I have a question.

Do you think that when you talk about the other self-fulfilling samadhi, and that's what, when Dogen says being illuminated by the myriad things, is that the same thing in the sense of what we're talking about?
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Yes.
Thank you all very much for listening.
